answer.rationale:
The binding constraints decide most of this. With 14 days to expiry, no auto-renew, and the line at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, any action that introduces qualification, tooling, or logistics transition inside this cycle is structurally unsafe regardless of how attractive its cost story looks. That rules out switch_primary_vendor now, even though memory_c2 reports a sharp unit-cost win from moving to the low-cost vendor: that record describes an onboarding under slack conditions, not a 14-day changeover against a fully loaded line, and cost-per-unit is not total cost of ownership if a single missed allocation stops assembly. It also rules out defer_decision, because memory_c5's month-to-month fallback applied to a non-critical service; here the contract does not auto-renew, so deferring means running the primary supply line without a contract. add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right structural move against single-point-of-failure risk but it is a qualification project, not a 14-day action, and it adds spend rather than cutting it — it should be the next review's decision.

That leaves negotiate_terms as the only lever that can touch the 18% mandate without moving physical supply. I chose to verify memory_c4 rather than the more tempting memory_c2 precisely because c4 is the memory my action rests on, and the summary is thin in the ways that matter: it says benchmarking 'moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms' but not the magnitude, not the leverage that made it work, and not whether that leverage existed because a credible alternative was ready. If the original record shows the recovery was a few points achieved with a qualified second vendor already in hand, then my position here is materially weaker — I have no credible walk-away, and the incumbent knows the expiry date and the volume commitment as well as I do.

Explicit residual risk: negotiation alone plausibly does not reach 18%. Memory_c6 offers multi-year volume pricing as the way to close a larger gap, and I am deliberately not committing to that shape yet — locking multiple years to hit this year's number would trade away exactly the optionality needed to qualify a second source or the low-cost vendor under non-emergency conditions, and would convert a one-cycle cost target into a multi-cycle dependency. Preferred structure is a short term with benchmarked pricing and an early-exit or volume-review clause, and I would rather report a shortfall against the 18% target than manufacture the number by mortgaging the next two cycles or by moving supply into a zero-buffer line. Memory_c1's stability record supports the incumbent as a safe bridge, not as a permanent answer.
